newsitem.title: CANADA: CIBC notes big drop in Q1 impaired loans.
newsitem.headline: CIBC notes big drop in Q1 impaired loans.

text.p: Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce said on Thursday it had experienced a "significant" drop in net impaired loans in the first quarter ending January 31, extending a decline seen last year.
"We expect a continuation of this trend in 1997 and have already seen some significant reductions so far this quarter," Chief Financial Officer John Doran told the bank's annual meeting.

Gerry Beasley, CIBC's senior vice president of risk managment, said a restructuring of debt by Olympia & York in November reduced the bank's impaired loans by about C$100 million. That was the most significant reduction so far in the first quarter, he said.
Asked if first quarter earnings would be higher than the C$1.53 a share the bank reported a year ago, chief executive Al Flood told reporters: "I expect it will be."
He also projected earnings for the 1997 fiscal year ending October 31 would rise from 1996's C$6.04 a share, but said the rate of increase would not be as great as in 1996.
"As far as the earnings are concerned, we see modest increases but nothing like we experienced in 1996...," Flood said. He said earnings grew by 35 percent in 1996.
The bank expects its loan loss provision to hold stable at around last year's level of C$480 million this year.

"We think the loan losses will probably remain about the same....We'll keep that 480 (million) pretty level," Flood said. Last year CIBC added C$93 million of that total to its general reserves and Flood said the bank would continue to seek to build its general reserves as a buffer for when the economy weakens.
He said the current economic climate of moderate growth, low inflation and low interest rates was favorable for financial services companies. "It is a growth industry," Flood said.

Asked about rumors that the bank's CIBC Wood Gundy unit was planning an acquisition in the United States, unit president John Hunkin said the investment bank would seek to "continue to build our capability in the United States" but that there was no specific acquisition currently planned.
He said CIBC Wood Gundy was targeting as clients non-investment grade companies in industries where it has expertise such as multimedia, technology, energy and natural resources.
Flood said the bank continues to aim for a 16 to 18 percent return on equity. Its 1996 ROE was 17.1 percent.
He said CIBC planned to boost its advertising.
